issues.title: The timezone plugin is not compatible with React Native Hermes engine
issues.body:
The timezone plugin throws a timezone RangeError error when calling .tz because React Native Hermes engine doesn't has support for Intl timezones and toLocaleString

This two lines are the ones that are throwing the error

https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs/blob/dev/src/plugin/timezone/index.js#L20

https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs/blob/dev/src/plugin/timezone/index.js#L98

Could be posible to update the plugin to not depend on Intl and toLocaleString('en-US', { timeZone: timezone }) ?

comments.body:
The above patch causes midnight dates to be formatted as `2010-01-01 24:00:00` after applying `.startOf("day")` (see [here](https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs/blob/v1.10.7/src/plugin/timezone/index.js#L123-L124)) once fed into the `Date` constructor by the `.tz` implementation (see [here](https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs/blob/v1.10.7/src/plugin/timezone/index.js#L98-L99)).

`24:00` marks the end of the day, leading the `Date` constructor to parse it as `Jan 02 2010 00:00:00 GMT+0100`. By replacing `hour12: false` with `hourCycle: "h23"` in the patch above the correct date is formatted / converted when using `.startOf("day")` in combination with timezones.

Before:
```
  const originalDay = dayjs("2010-01-01T00:00:00Z").tz("UTC")
  const startOfDay = originalDay.startOf("day")
  console.log(startOfDay.valueOf() === originalDay.valueOf()) // false using above patch
```

After:
```
  const originalDay = dayjs("2010-01-01T00:00:00Z").tz("UTC")
  const startOfDay = originalDay.startOf("day")
  console.log(startOfDay.valueOf() === originalDay.valueOf()) // true, using above patch with hourCycle: "h23" instead of hour12: false
```

issues.title: Cannot strict parse date with timezone (ZZ)
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

Parsing a date in strict mode (with `customParseFormat` plugin) with [timezone (ZZ / +0600)](https://day.js.org/docs/en/parse/string-format#:~:text=ZZ) returns a date object which is not `.isValid()`.

```
const dayjs = require("dayjs");
const customParseFormat = require("dayjs/plugin/customParseFormat");

dayjs.extend(customParseFormat);

const dateFormat = "YYYYMMDD HHmmss ZZ";

const date = dayjs("20241224 061500 +0600", dateFormat);
console.log("date.isValid()", date.isValid()); // true

My investigation points to the same root cause.
1. For 0 offset timezones, date is marked as UTC:
https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs/blame/v1.11.13/src/plugin/utc/index.js#L93

Values  this.$y, this.$M, this.$D, this.$W, this.$H etc. remains unchanged (local).

2. When calling "set", it clones the whole object first, and down the chain, it calls "parse", which assigns UTC values to this.$y, this.$M etc. Similary, when calling "locale" it calls "clone" down the chain.

https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs/blob/v1.11.13/src/plugin/utc/index.js#L56

3. As a result  this.$y, this.$M etc. are misaligned with $d (native Date object).

Simple case to reproduce:

Set your PC timezone to other than 0 offset, then:
```
import dayjs from 'dayjs';
import timezone from 'dayjs/plugin/timezone';
import utc from 'dayjs/plugin/utc';

dayjs.extend(utc);
dayjs.extend(timezone);

const London1 = dayjs().tz('Europe/London');
const London2 = dayjs().tz('Europe/London').clone();

console.log('London2: ' + London2.format('DD HH:mm:ss Z')); // London2: 11 07:33:00 +00:00
```

By default, **Day.js** uses a *lenient parsing mode* and will try to parse a datetime input as much as possible, even if the values are not strictly valid.

If you need **strict parsing**, you may have to:

1. Tell Day.js the exact format to parse.
2. Enable the strict flag by passing `true` as the third argument.

```js
import dayjs from 'dayjs'
import customParseFormat from 'dayjs/plugin/customParseFormat'

dayjs.extend(customParseFormat)

const strictDate = dayjs('2025-13-36T14:19:39', 'YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss', true)
console.log(strictDate.isValid()) // false
```

issues.title: customParseFormat: week token ('w'/'ww') is silently ignored when parsing with dayjs.utc()
issues.body:
**Describe the bug**

When parsing a date string that contains a week-of-year token (`w` or `ww`) using `dayjs.utc(input, format)` together with the `customParseFormat` plugin, the parsed week number is silently discarded and the resulting date defaults to week 1 of the year.

This is the same underlying issue that was fixed for non-UTC parsing in #2705 (released in 1.11.13), but the fix was only applied to the local-time branch of `parseFormattedInput`, not the UTC branch.

Looking at `src/plugin/customParseFormat/index.js`:

```js
if (utc) {
  return new Date(Date.UTC(y, M, d, h, m, s, ms))   // <-- returns before `week` is ever used
}
let newDate = new Date(y, M, d, h, m, s, ms)
if (week) {
  newDate = dayjs(newDate).week(week).toDate()        // <-- week is only applied here
}
return newDate
```

The `if (utc)` branch returns immediately and never checks the `week` variable, so any week number parsed from the input string is lost when using `dayjs.utc()`.

**To Reproduce**

```js
import dayjs from 'dayjs'
import utc from 'dayjs/plugin/utc'
import weekOfYear from 'dayjs/plugin/weekOfYear'
import customParseFormat from 'dayjs/plugin/customParseFormat'

dayjs.extend(utc)
dayjs.extend(weekOfYear)
dayjs.extend(customParseFormat)

// Local mode: works correctly (fixed in 1.11.13 / #2705)
console.log(dayjs('2024-31', 'YYYY-ww').format('YYYY-ww'))      // 2024-31 ✅

// UTC mode: week is ignored
console.log(dayjs.utc('2024-31', 'YYYY-ww').format('YYYY-ww'))  // 2024-01 ❌
```

**Expected behavior**


dayjs.utc('2024-31', 'YYYY-ww').format('YYYY-ww')
// should return "2024-31", matching the behavior already fixed for non-UTC parsing


**Suggested fix**

Apply the same `week` handling before branching on `utc`, e.g.:

```js
let newDate = utc
  ? new Date(Date.UTC(y, M, d, h, m, s, ms))
  : new Date(y, M, d, h, m, s, ms)

if (week) {
  newDate = (utc ? dayjs.utc(newDate) : dayjs(newDate)).week(week).toDate()
}

return newDate
```

**Information**

- Day.js Version: 1.11.19 (latest, verified in source on `dev` branch — the UTC branch has not been updated since the 1.11.13 fix)
- Plugins used: `utc`, `weekOfYear`, `customParseFormat`
- Environment: Node.js / any (logic bug, not environment-specific)

comments.body:
Confirmed this still reproduces in **Day.js 1.11.23** (current npm latest), as well as **1.11.13**, through the public `dayjs.tz(string, zone)` API. Here is a minimal reproduction with no mocks or application code.

### Reproduction

```sh
mkdir dayjs-zero-offset-repro
cd dayjs-zero-offset-repro
npm init -y
npm install dayjs@1.11.23
```

Save as `repro.cjs`:

```js
const dayjs = require('dayjs');
dayjs.extend(require('dayjs/plugin/utc'));
dayjs.extend(require('dayjs/plugin/timezone'));

console.log(dayjs.tz('2026-10-24 19:30', 'America/Los_Angeles').toISOString());
console.log(dayjs.tz('2026-03-29 09:30', 'Asia/Tokyo').toISOString());
```

Run in separate processes:

```sh
TZ=Europe/London node repro.cjs
TZ=UTC node repro.cjs
```

Expected in **both** environments:

```text
2026-10-25T02:30:00.000Z
2026-03-29T00:30:00.000Z
```

Actual with `TZ=Europe/London`:

```text
2026-10-25T03:30:00.000Z
2026-03-29T01:30:00.000Z
```

`TZ=UTC` gives the expected results. Both target wall-clock times are unambiguous: this is not a gap/overlap in the explicitly selected target timezone. The result incorrectly depends on the host timezone.

### Diagnosis

Tracing the first example in 1.11.13, the timezone plugin initially computes the correct instant `2026-10-25T02:30:00.000Z`, then calls `d(targetTs).utcOffset(targetOffset)`.

At that point:

- `targetOffset` is `-420`.
- The stored `$x.$localOffset` is `0`: London has already returned to GMT at the target instant.
- The intermediate `$d` represents `2026-10-24T19:30:00.000Z`, when London was still on daylight saving time; `$d.getTimezoneOffset()` is `-60`.
- In `valueOf()`, `$x.$localOffset || $d.getTimezoneOffset()` discards the valid `0` and uses `-60`, shifting the resulting timestamp by one hour.

Source references: [timezone factory](https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs/blob/v1.11.13/src/plugin/timezone/index.js#L132-L135), [utcOffset](https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs/blob/v1.11.13/src/plugin/utc/index.js#L90-L95), [valueOf](https://github.com/iamkun/dayjs/blob/v1.11.13/src/plugin/utc/index.js#L108-L111).

Using nullish selection instead of `||` in a standalone diagnostic calculation restores the expected timestamp for this case. This is **not** a claim that changing that expression alone fully fixes formatting or all related behavior; those paths need separate regression coverage.

### Tested scope

On 1.11.13, both cases above are one hour late with host zones `Europe/London`, `Europe/Dublin`, `Europe/Lisbon`, and `Atlantic/Canary`. The same cases are correct with `UTC`, `Atlantic/Reykjavik`, `Europe/Berlin`, `America/Los_Angeles`, and `Asia/Shanghai`. An ordinary-date control case is correct. Both the London and UTC cases were also rerun on 1.11.23 with the results shown above.

Environment: Node.js v24.18.0, macOS 27.0.1, using the `TZ` environment variable per process. No browser reproduction or other Day.js versions are claimed here.

**Description:**

In the Arabic locale (ar), the L date format includes Right-to-Left Mark characters (RLM, U+200F). These characters are intended to control text direction, but in Arabic typography, numbers and dates are written left-to-right and should not have their direction altered.

Including RLM in the format produces several problems:

- The RLM characters are unnecessary for correct Arabic formatting.
- When rendered in HTML, these hidden characters often cause the order of day, month, and year to appear incorrectly.

The Arabic locale format L should not contain RLM characters. Dates should display naturally without forcing direction changes.

I'm not 100% sure I understand your issue, but to me, everything seems correct.

If you take a look at https://www.epochconverter.com/weeks/2021, the first ISO week of 2021 began on January 4th 2021. Therefore, any dates before then would then should reference week 30 of 2020 (which started on July 20th 2020).

As for the dates incrementing, this is due to dayjs choosing the offset to use based on the day of the week, and not the date itself when using isoWeek.

January 1st 2021 was a Friday, and the Friday in week 30 of 2020 was July 24th 2020. January 2nd was Saturday in 2021, and Saturday in week 30 of 2020 was July 25th 2020 (etc.).

JavaScript Date objects internally represent time as a UTC timestamp — a single point on the timeline. They don’t store any timezone information. When you create a date like:

comments.body:
Hi @SuperPanda911,

I understand this can be confusing however, this stems from how the **built-in JS Date constructor** parses strings.

When we call `dayjs("dall-e-3")`, dayjs internally falls back to `new Date("dall-e-3")` as it does not match the ISO 8601 pattern.

Since `new Date("dall-e-3")` returns a valid (but unintended) date, dayjs reports it as valid too.

I'd recommend specifying the format `dayjs('dall-e-3', 'MM/DD/YYYY')` for stricter validation, or if not possible adding your own validation logic before passing arbitrary strings to dayjs.

Hope this helps!
